question: ¿Cómo cambio el puerto HTTP de mi aplicación Spring Boot y cuál es el valor por defecto?
ground_truth: El puerto HTTP por defecto es 8080. Se cambia con la propiedad server.port (por ejemplo en application.properties). Con server.port=0 se busca un puerto libre y con server.port=-1 se desactivan los endpoints HTTP.
response:
### Respuesta
El puerto HTTP por defecto es el `8080` [3]. Puedes cambiarlo utilizando la propiedad `server.port` (por ejemplo, en `application.properties` o como una propiedad de sistema) [3]. Gracias a la vinculación flexible (*relaxed binding*) de los valores del `Environment`, también puedes usar la variable de entorno del sistema operativo `SERVER_PORT` [3]. Además, puedes usar `server.port=0` para elegir un puerto aleatorio no utilizado o `server.port=-1` para desactivar completamente los endpoints HTTP [3].
contexts:

Spring MVC uses the HttpMessageConverter interface to convert HTTP requests and responses.
Sensible defaults are included out of the box.
For example, objects can be automatically converted to JSON (by using the Jackson library) or XML (by using the Jackson XML extension, if available, or by using JAXB if the Jackson XML extension is not available).
By default, strings are encoded in UTF-8 .
Any HttpMessageConverter bean that is present in the context is added to the list of converters.
You can also override default converters in the same way.

Spring Boot How-to - Embedded Web Servers > Change the HTTP Port
In a standalone application, the main HTTP port defaults to 8080 but can be set with server.port (for example, in application.properties or as a System property).
Thanks to relaxed binding of Environment values, you can also use SERVER_PORT (for example, as an OS environment variable).
To switch off the HTTP endpoints completely but still create a WebApplicationContext , use server.port=-1 (doing so is sometimes useful for testing).
For more details, see Customizing Embedded Servlet Containers in the ‘Spring Boot Features’ section, or the ServerProperties class.

question: Web server failed to start. Port 8080 was already in use. ¿Qué puedo hacer?
ground_truth: El puerto 8080, que es el predeterminado, ya está siendo usado por otro proceso. Se puede cambiar el puerto de la aplicación con la propiedad server.port en application.properties, o usar server.port=0 para que se asigne un puerto libre.
response:
### Diagnóstico
La aplicación no puede iniciar porque el puerto predeterminado 8080 está siendo utilizado por otro proceso [1].

### Posibles causas
- Otra aplicación o instancia de tu proyecto ya está ocupando el puerto 8080 [1].

### Qué revisaría primero
1. Cambiar el puerto HTTP usando la propiedad `server.port` (por ejemplo, en `application.properties` o como propiedad del sistema) [1].
2. Usar la variable de entorno del sistema operativo `SERVER_PORT` gracias al binding relajado de los valores del `Environment` [1].
3. Configurar `server.port=0` para buscar un puerto libre no asignado usando funciones nativas del sistema operativo [4].

### Información que hace falta
Ninguna para esta comprobación inicial.

question: ¿Cómo activo un perfil de Spring en una aplicación Spring Boot?
ground_truth: Con la propiedad spring.profiles.active, por ejemplo spring.profiles.active=dev,hsqldb en application.properties, o por línea de comandos con --spring.profiles.active=dev,hsqldb. Si no hay ningún perfil activo se habilita el perfil llamado default.
response:
### Respuesta
Puedes activar un perfil de Spring Boot de las siguientes maneras:
- Configurando una propiedad del sistema o una variable de entorno con `spring.profiles.active` o `SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE` [3].
- Usando un argumento `-D` al arrancar la aplicación (colocándolo antes de la clase principal o del archivo jar), por ejemplo: `java -jar -Dspring.profiles.active=production demo-0.0.1-SNAPSHOT.jar` [3].
- Definiéndolo en el archivo `application.properties` como `spring.profiles.active=production` o en YAML como `spring.profiles.active: "production"` [3].
- Programáticamente, llamando a `SpringApplication.setAdditionalProfiles(...)` antes de que la aplicación se ejecute o utilizando la interfaz `ConfigurableEnvironment` de Spring [1].

question: ¿Qué es un grupo de perfiles y cómo se define?
ground_truth: Un grupo de perfiles permite definir un nombre lógico para un conjunto de perfiles relacionados. Por ejemplo, con spring.profiles.group.production[0]=proddb y spring.profiles.group.production[1]=prodmq, al activar el perfil production se activan también proddb y prodmq.
response:
### Respuesta
Un grupo de perfiles es una característica de Spring Boot que permite definir un nombre lógico para un grupo relacionado de perfiles [1]. Esto ayuda a evitar que los perfiles sean demasiado detallados y difíciles de usar cuando se tienen, por ejemplo, perfiles independientes para bases de datos y mensajería [1].

Se puede definir utilizando propiedades en formato `application.properties` o mediante YAML [1]. Por ejemplo, para crear un grupo llamado `production` que agrupe los perfiles `proddb` y `prodmq`, se puede configurar de las siguientes maneras [1]:

En `application.properties`:
```properties
spring.profiles.group.production[0]=proddb
spring.profiles.group.production[1]=prodmq
```[1]

En YAML:
```yaml
spring:
  profiles:
    group:
      production:
      - "proddb"
      - "prodmq"
```[1]
contexts:
Spring Boot - Profiles > Profile Groups
Occasionally the profiles that you define and use in your application are too fine-grained and become cumbersome to use.
For example, you might have proddb and prodmq profiles that you use to enable database and messaging features independently.
To help with this, Spring Boot lets you define profile groups.
A profile group allows you to define a logical name for a related group of profiles.
For example, we can create a production group that consists of our proddb and prodmq profiles.
Properties
YAML
```
spring.profiles.group.production[0]=proddb
spring.profiles.group.production[1]=prodmq
```
```
spring:
  profiles:
    group:
      production:
      - "proddb"
      - "prodmq"
```

```

The <SpringProfile> tag can contain a profile name (for example staging ) or a profile expression.
A profile expression allows for more complicated profile logic to be expressed, for example production & (eu-central | eu-west) .

question: ¿Cómo configuro el nivel de log de un paquete y del logger raíz?
ground_truth: Se usa logging.level.<nombre-del-logger>=<nivel>, donde el nivel puede ser TRACE, DEBUG, INFO, WARN, ERROR, FATAL u OFF. El logger raíz se configura con logging.level.root.
response:
### Respuesta
Los niveles de los loggers se pueden configurar en el Spring Environment (por ejemplo, en `application.properties`) usando la propiedad `logging.level.<logger-name>=<level>`, donde el nivel puede ser `TRACE`, `DEBUG`, `INFO`, `WARN`, `ERROR`, `FATAL` o `OFF` [1]. 

Para configurar específicamente el logger raíz (root logger), se debe utilizar `logging.level.root` [1]. 

Un ejemplo de configuración en `application.properties` es:
```properties
logging.level.root=warn
logging.level.org.springframework.web=debug
logging.level.org.hibernate=error
```
[1]

También es posible establecer los niveles de log mediante variables de entorno, por ejemplo utilizando `LOGGING_LEVEL_ORG_SPRINGFRAMEWORK_WEB=DEBUG` [1].

question: ¿Cómo hago que Spring Boot escriba los logs en un archivo?
ground_truth: Por defecto Spring Boot solo registra en la consola. Para escribir archivos de log hay que definir la propiedad logging.file.name o logging.file.path. Si se definen ambas, logging.file.path se ignora y solo se usa logging.file.name.
response:
### Respuesta
Para que Spring Boot escriba logs en un archivo además de la salida en consola, debes configurar la propiedad `logging.file.name` o `logging.file.path` (por ejemplo, en tu `application.properties`) [3]. 

Ten en cuenta lo siguiente:
- Por defecto, Spring Boot solo registra en la consola y no escribe archivos de log [3].
- Si configuras ambas propiedades (`logging.file.name` y `logging.file.path`), `logging.file.path` será ignorada y solo se usará `logging.file.name` [3].
- El valor de `logging.file.name` puede ser una ruta absoluta o relativa al directorio actual [3].

question: ¿Qué endpoints de Actuator están expuestos por defecto y cómo expongo otros?
ground_truth: Por defecto solo el endpoint health está expuesto por HTTP y JMX. Para exponer otros se usan las propiedades de inclusión y exclusión, como management.endpoints.web.exposure.include para HTTP y management.endpoints.jmx.exposure.include para JMX.
response:
### Respuesta
Por defecto, solo el endpoint `/health` está expuesto sobre HTTP y JMX [1, 2]. 

Para exponer otros endpoints, se debe utilizar la propiedad `management.endpoints.web.exposure.include` [1, 2].
contexts:
Spring Boot - Actuator Endpoints > Security
For security purposes, only the /health endpoint is exposed over HTTP by default.
You can use the management.endpoints.web.exposure.include property to configure the endpoints that are exposed.
 | Before setting the management.endpoints.web.exposure.include , ensure that the exposed actuators do not contain sensitive information, are secured by placing them behind a firewall, or are secured by something like Spring Security.
If Spring Security is on the classpath and no other SecurityFilterChain bean is present, all actuators other than /health are secured by Spring Boot auto-configuration.
If you define a custom SecurityFilterChain bean, Spring Boot auto-configuration backs off and lets you fully control the actuator access rules.

Spring Boot - Actuator Endpoints > Exposing Endpoints
By default, only the health endpoint is exposed over HTTP and JMX.
Since Endpoints may contain sensitive information, you should carefully consider when to expose them.
To change which endpoints are exposed, use the following technology-specific include and exclude properties:
Property | Default
management.endpoints.jmx.exposure.exclude | 
management.endpoints.jmx.exposure.include | health
management.endpoints.web.exposure.exclude | 
management.endpoints.web.exposure.include | health
The include property lists the IDs of the endpoints that are exposed.
The exclude property lists the IDs of the endpoints that should not be exposed.
The exclude property takes precedence over the include property.
You can configure both the include and the exclude properties with a list of endpoint IDs.

Spring Boot - Actuator Endpoints > Custom Web Endpoints
Operations on an @Endpoint , @WebEndpoint , or @EndpointWebExtension are automatically exposed over HTTP using Jersey, Spring MVC, or Spring WebFlux.
If both Jersey and Spring MVC are available, Spring MVC is used.
A request predicate is automatically generated for each operation on a web-exposed endpoint.
The path of the predicate is determined by the ID of the endpoint and the base path of the web-exposed endpoints.
The default base path is /actuator .
For example, an endpoint with an ID of sessions uses /actuator/sessions as its path in the predicate.
You can further customize the path by annotating one or more parameters of the operation method with @Selector .
Such a parameter is added to the path predicate as a path variable.

Spring Boot - Actuator Endpoints > Endpoints
Actuator endpoints let you monitor and interact with your application.
Spring Boot includes a number of built-in endpoints and lets you add your own.
For example, the health endpoint provides basic application health information.
You can control access to each individual endpoint and expose them (make them remotely accessible) over HTTP or JMX .
An endpoint is considered to be available when access to it is permitted and it is exposed.
The built-in endpoints are auto-configured only when they are available.
Most applications choose exposure over HTTP, where the ID of the endpoint and a prefix of /actuator is mapped to a URL.
For example, by default, the health endpoint is mapped to /actuator/health .

question: ¿Cómo expone Spring Boot el estado de liveness y readiness para Kubernetes?
ground_truth: En un entorno Kubernetes, Actuator obtiene la información de liveness y readiness de la interfaz ApplicationAvailability y la expone con los indicadores de salud LivenessStateHealthIndicator y ReadinessStateHealthIndicator, que aparecen en el endpoint global /actuator/health.
response:
### Respuesta
Spring Boot gestiona por defecto el estado de disponibilidad (*Application Availability*) de la aplicación y recopila la información de "Liveness" y "Readiness" a través de la interfaz `ApplicationAvailability` [1]. 

Esta información se expone de las siguientes maneras:
- Se muestra de forma conjunta en el endpoint global de salud (`/actuator/health`) mediante los indicadores `LivenessStateHealthIndicator` y `ReadinessStateHealthIndicator` [1].
- Se expone mediante sondas HTTP separadas usando grupos de salud en las rutas `/actuator/health/liveness` y `/actuator/health/readiness` [1].
- Las sondas escuchan eventos del ciclo de vida de la aplicación durante el arranque y el apagado para reflejar el estado interno (`AvailabilityState`) y el estado de los conectores HTTP [2].
contexts:
Spring Boot - Actuator Endpoints > Kubernetes Probes
Applications deployed on Kubernetes can provide information about their internal state with Container Probes .
Depending on your Kubernetes configuration , the kubelet calls those probes and reacts to the result.
By default, Spring Boot manages your Application Availability state.
If deployed in a Kubernetes environment, actuator gathers the “Liveness” and “Readiness” information from the ApplicationAvailability interface and uses that information in dedicated health indicators : LivenessStateHealthIndicator and ReadinessStateHealthIndicator .
These indicators are shown on the global health endpoint ( "/actuator/health" ).
They are also exposed as separate HTTP Probes by using health groups : "/actuator/health/liveness" and "/actuator/health/readiness" .

Spring Boot - Actuator Endpoints > Application Lifecycle and Probe States
An important aspect of the Kubernetes Probes support is its consistency with the application lifecycle.
There is a significant difference between the AvailabilityState (which is the in-memory, internal state of the application)
and the actual probe (which exposes that state).
Depending on the phase of application lifecycle, the probe might not be available.
Spring Boot publishes application events during startup and shutdown ,
and probes can listen to such events and expose the AvailabilityState information.
The following tables show the AvailabilityState and the state of HTTP connectors at different stages.
When a Spring Boot application starts:
Startup phase | LivenessState | ReadinessState | HTTP server | Notes

Spring Boot - Actuator Endpoints > Kubernetes Probes
You can then configure your Kubernetes infrastructure with the following endpoint information:
```
livenessProbe:
  httpGet:
    path: "/actuator/health/liveness"
    port: <actuator-port>
  failureThreshold: ...
  periodSeconds: ...

Spring Boot - Actuator Endpoints > Application Lifecycle and Probe States
When a Spring Boot application starts:
Startup phase | LivenessState | ReadinessState | HTTP server | Notes
Starting | BROKEN | REFUSING_TRAFFIC | Not started | Kubernetes checks the "liveness" Probe and restarts the application if it takes too long.
Started | CORRECT | REFUSING_TRAFFIC | Refuses requests | The application context is refreshed. The application performs startup tasks and does not receive traffic yet.
Ready | CORRECT | ACCEPTING_TRAFFIC | Accepts requests | Startup tasks are finished. The application is receiving traffic.
When a Spring Boot application shuts down:
Shutdown phase | Liveness State | Readiness State | HTTP server | Notes
Running | CORRECT | ACCEPTING_TRAFFIC | Accepts requests | Shutdown has been requested.

question: ¿Cuándo hace rollback @Transactional por defecto?
ground_truth: Por defecto cualquier RuntimeException o Error provoca rollback, mientras que las excepciones comprobadas (checked) no lo provocan. Este comportamiento por defecto se puede cambiar.
response:
### Respuesta

- Inyección basada en setter (*setter-based dependency injection*), realizada mediante la llamada a métodos setter por parte del contenedor después de invocar un constructor o método de fábrica sin argumentos [4], recomendada principalmente para dependencias opcionales [1, 2].

Spring Boot How-to - Data Access > Use Spring Data Repositories
To get started, create some repository interfaces to handle your @Entity objects.
Spring Boot determines the location of your Repository implementations by scanning the auto-configuration packages .
For more control, use the @Enable…Repositories annotations from Spring Data.
For more about Spring Data, see the Spring Data project page .

Spring Boot How-to - Data Access > Customize Spring Data’s Web Support
Spring Data provides web support that simplifies the use of Spring Data repositories in a web application.
Spring Boot provides properties in the spring.data.web namespace for customizing its configuration.
Note that if you are using Spring Data REST, you must use the properties in the spring.data.rest namespace instead.

Spring Boot - SQL Databases > Connection to a JNDI DataSource
If you deploy your Spring Boot application to an Application Server, you might want to configure and manage your DataSource by using your Application Server’s built-in features and access it by using JNDI.
The spring.datasource.jndi-name property can be used as an alternative to the spring.datasource.url , spring.datasource.username , and spring.datasource.password properties to access the DataSource from a specific JNDI location.
For example, the following section in application.properties shows how you can access a JBoss AS defined DataSource :
Properties
YAML
```
spring.datasource.jndi-name=java:jboss/datasources/customers
```
```
spring:
  datasource:
    jndi-name: "java:jboss/datasources/customers"
```

Spring Boot How-to - Properties and Configuration > Properties and Configuration
This section includes topics about setting and reading properties and configuration settings and their interaction with Spring Boot applications.

Spring Boot - Auto-configuration > Auto-configuration
Spring Boot auto-configuration attempts to automatically configure your Spring application based on the jar dependencies that you have added.
For example, if HSQLDB is on your classpath, and you have not manually configured any database connection beans, then Spring Boot auto-configures an in-memory database.
You need to opt-in to auto-configuration by adding the @EnableAutoConfiguration or @SpringBootApplication annotations to one of your @Configuration classes.
 | You should only ever add one @SpringBootApplication or @EnableAutoConfiguration annotation.
We generally recommend that you add one or the other to your primary @Configuration class only.

Spring Boot - Externalized Configuration > Enabling @ConfigurationProperties-annotated Types
Spring Boot provides infrastructure to bind @ConfigurationProperties types and register them as beans.
You can either enable configuration properties on a class-by-class basis or enable configuration property scanning that works in a similar manner to component scanning.
Sometimes, classes annotated with @ConfigurationProperties might not be suitable for scanning, for example, if you’re developing your own auto-configuration or you want to enable them conditionally.
In these cases, specify the list of types to process using the @EnableConfigurationProperties annotation.
